## Q1 | A Monopoly on Brooms

In the early days of the broomstick market, CloudSweep was the only maker of the standard broom. As in Homework E1, it has high fixed costs, 1,000 coins a week, and a constant marginal cost: each broom costs 15 coins more to make, so $MC = 15$. As the only seller it faces the whole market’s demand and charges the same price for every broom. Demand and marginal revenue are:

$$
D: P = 135 - Q \qquad\qquad MR = 135 - 2Q
$$

where $Q$ is the number of brooms it makes in a week. Each graph shows demand and marginal cost.

:::: {.columns gutter=0.5em}

::: {.column width=60%}

CloudSweep picks its quantity and price:

a\) Graph marginal revenue ($MR$).

::: solution

$MR = 135 - 2Q$ starts at 135 with demand and falls twice as fast: it is 15 at 60 brooms and reaches zero at 67.5.

:::

b\) Find and graph the profit-maximizing quantity ($Q^*$).

::: solution

$MR = MC$: $135 - 2Q = 15$, so $2Q = 120$ and $Q^* = 60$ brooms.

:::

c\) Find and graph the price that sells that quantity ($P^*$).

::: solution

Go up to demand at 60 brooms: $P^* = 135 - 60 = 75$ coins.

:::

d\) Find CloudSweep’s maximized profit.

::: solution

Each broom brings in $75 - 15 = 60$ coins over its marginal cost, so $60 \times 60 = 3{,}600$, less the fixed costs of 1,000: a profit of 2,600 coins.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

:::

::::

:::: {.columns gutter=0.5em}

::: {.column width=60%}

There are no externalities:

e\) Find and graph the socially efficient quantity.

::: solution

Demand crosses $MC$ where $135 - Q = 15$, so $Q = 120$ brooms.

:::

f\) Find and shade the deadweight loss.

::: solution

The triangle between demand and $MC$ from 60 to 120: $\frac{1}{2}(75 - 15)(120 - 60) = 1{,}800$ coins.

:::

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

:::

## Q2 | The History of the Broomstick Market

In the early days of magical sporting and transportation, CloudSweep was the first broomstick maker to enter the market. They developed a proprietary method for autolocomotion and held the entirety of the market. As their technological secrets began disseminating among the wizarding world, many broomstick makers began producing broomsticks with identical handling and acceleration characteristics. Today, few if any new broomstick makers had opened.

Using a few graphs to illustrate your answer, tell the story of the evolution of the broomstick market from it’s inception to the present. Be sure to finish in a long run equilibrium.

::: solution

**One seller.** CloudSweep is the only seller, as in Q1, so it faces the whole market’s demand. It sells the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, $Q_M$, and charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity, $P_M$. That price is above its cost and it earns a profit. It also sells too little: less than $Q_{SC}$, the efficient quantity where demand meets marginal cost. The trades it leaves out are a deadweight loss.

**Entry.** Once the secret is out, anyone can make an identical broom. CloudSweep’s profit draws makers in. Each new maker adds to market supply, so the price falls, and with identical brooms no maker can charge more than the others: every maker becomes a price taker.

**Long run.** Entry continues as long as makers earn a profit. It stops when the price has fallen to the lowest point of average total cost, $P_{LR}$. Each maker produces where $P = MC = ATC$ and earns zero economic profit, which is why few if any new makers open today. Compared with the start, the price is lower, the market quantity is larger, and the market now produces the efficient quantity $Q^*$ at the lowest average total cost.

:::
